lesson.title: Character Encoding: How Letters Become Numbers
lesson.summary: Explains how computers, which only store bits, represent text by assigning each character a numeric code, building on prior knowledge of bits and bytes.
lesson.body:
A computer's memory only ever stores bits, the binary digits 0 and 1, grouped together in bytes of eight bits each. As you already know from bits and bytes, a single byte can represent 256 distinct values, since there are 2 to the 8th power possible combinations of eight binary digits. That fact raises an obvious question: if a computer can only store numbers, how does it store and display text, like the letters you are reading right now? The answer is character encoding, a system that assigns a specific numeric code to every character a computer needs to represent, including letters, digits, punctuation, and even the space character. Everything you have ever typed, and everything a computer has ever displayed as text, ultimately exists in memory as nothing more than sequences of these numeric codes, stored as bits.

Character encoding is fundamentally an agreement. There is nothing inherent in the number 65 that makes it mean the letter A. Instead, everyone who builds software agrees to use the same mapping, so that when one program stores the number 65 intending it to mean A, every other program that reads that number also interprets it as A. Without this shared agreement, text saved by one program could look like meaningless numbers, or the wrong letters entirely, when opened by another.

Python gives direct access to this mapping through two built in functions, ord and chr. ord takes a single character and returns its numeric code, while chr does the reverse, taking a number and returning the corresponding character. For example:

print(ord('A'))
print(chr(65))
print(ord('a'))

Running this code prints 65, then A, then 97. The first line reveals that the character 'A' is stored using the numeric code 65. The second line demonstrates the reverse relationship: given the number 65, chr reconstructs the character A. The third line shows something important, that 'a', the lowercase version of the same letter, has a completely different code, 97, not 65. Uppercase and lowercase letters are treated as entirely distinct characters in this scheme, each with its own independent numeric code, which is why comparisons like 'A' == 'a' evaluate to False in Python.

This numeric code is small enough, in the most common cases, to fit inside a single byte, since 65 and 97 both fall well within the range 0 to 255 that a byte can represent. But which numbers get assigned to which characters, and whether one byte is even enough to cover every character in every language, depends on the specific character encoding standard being used. The most historically important of these standards, and the one that established the numeric codes used in the examples above, is ASCII, which is the subject of the next section. Every text file, every string variable in a running Python program, and every character sent across a network is, underneath, relying on some agreed upon encoding just like this one.
